title: A Wannier-first approach for extended chiral systems
authors: Yashpal Singh, Juan E. Peralta, Koblar A. Jackson, Mark R. Pederson
abstract: We present a real-space formulation of DFT for extended systems in which localized Wannier-like functions are constructed directly from localized Gaussian basis functions without explicitly computing canonical Bloch-like states during the self-consistent cycle. Building on the formalism of Pederson and Lin [Phys. Rev. B \textbf{35}, 2273 (1987)], a variational set of Wannier-like functions is generated self-consistently within a finite Wannier domain and used to construct the charge density, electrostatic potential, and per cell total energy of the extended system. The occupied space can be determined entirely from the Wannier-like functions. Electronic band structures can be recovered in a post-processing step by solving the full Hamiltonian in a Bloch-like basis constructed from Gaussian orbitals. A key feature of the method is that it can incorporate combined translation--rotation, or screw, symmetries, enabling efficient simulations of chiral and helical systems with finite twist angles at essentially the same computational cost as systems described by pure translational symmetry. The approach is validated through calculations on linear and twisted $\mathrm{{-}C{\equiv}C{-}}$ and $\mathrm{{-}Li{-}F{-}}$ chains, as well as graphene, where total energies and band structures show excellent agreement with reference periodic calculations. To illustrate the ability of the method to treat three-dimensional systems, it is further applied to AA graphite, in which carbon atoms in adjacent graphene layers are aligned directly above one another, as well as helically stacked AA graphite structures. The Wannier-first framework provides a practical route for treating extended systems with nontrivial translational, rotational, and screw symmetries, and provides a natural foundation for the implementation of orbital-dependent functionals such as the Perdew--Zunger self-interaction correction.
summary: This paper introduces a 'Wannier-first' approach to DFT, enabling the simulation of extended chiral and helical materials by constructing localized Wannier-like functions directly in real space. This method efficiently handles complex symmetries, such as screw rotations, without the computational cost of large supercells. It provides a robust, practical framework for studying materials with nontrivial periodic symmetries.
main_problem: Developing an efficient electronic structure method for extended chiral systems that can accurately incorporate complex symmetries like screw rotations without resorting to prohibitively large supercells.
main_result: The Wannier-first approach successfully calculates total energies and band structures for various chiral and layered materials, showing excellent agreement with reference periodic calculations.
method: It uses a real-space, Wannier-like function construction within a finite Wannier domain, avoiding the explicit calculation of Bloch states during the self-consistent field (SCF) cycle.
model_or_system: The method is applied to extended periodic systems, including chiral chains ($	ext{-C}\equiv	ext{C}	ext{-}$, $	ext{-Li-F-}$), graphene, and layered graphite structures, allowing for the natural inclusion of combined translation-rotation (screw) symmetries.
key_observables: Total energies, band structures, band gaps ($E_g$), and energy differences ($\delta E$).
important_parameters: The size of the Wannier Domain (WD) and the convergence threshold ($\epsilon = 10^{-5}$ Hartree).
main_assumptions: The contribution of Wannier-like functions outside the finite Wannier Domain is negligible for charge density calculation.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the Wannier domain and localized functions; Figure 2 shows the iterative flowchart for SCF convergence; Table I compares calculated band gaps and energy differences across various systems and twist angles.
paper_structure: The paper details the formalism, building upon previous work, by defining the Wannier-like function optimization ($\hat{\Pi}$ operator), outlining the SCF procedure using the localized basis, and finally applying the method to benchmark systems to validate its capability with complex symmetries.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state DFT, the core numerical technique—constructing localized basis sets and solving physics problems in a real-space, symmetry-adapted manner—is highly relevant for simulating open quantum systems or molecular dynamics where localized representations are preferred over Bloch wavefunctions.
